references.text: Ishmael, the son of the slave woman Hagar, was driven away by Sarah because he should not inherit together with Isaac. Similarly, Jephthah was driven away by his half-brothers because he was the son of another woman.
Abraham sent away the sons of his concubines with gifts, but the inheritance went to Isaac. This shows a pattern where sons of secondary wives or other women were excluded from inheritance.

Hagar was a slave woman who bore Ishmael for Abraham. Jephthah's mother was also a woman of lower status (a prostitute), and both sons experienced conflicts related to inheritance and family position.

Abimelech, the son of Gideon's concubine, also had a complicated family background and fought for a position among his brothers. This shows a similar pattern of family conflicts regarding sons of secondary wives.
Paul uses the story of Ishmael and Isaac as an allegory, where the one born according to the flesh persecuted the one born according to the Spirit. Jephthah's exclusion follows the same pattern.
Jephthah is mentioned among the heroes of faith despite his difficult background and rejection by his family. His faith overcame the social obstacles he faced.
